# Project Architecture

Produce an ARCHITECTURE.md defining high-level technical structure, components, and technology choices, through guided conversation.

This is a **high-abstraction** document: it describes _what_ the system is made of and _why_, not _how_ it's coded. Never include code examples, file names, directory paths, or specific version numbers; those belong in implementation specs and task plans.

A finished ARCHITECTURE.md names the main components and their responsibilities, the data architecture, the technology stack with rationale, and the key decisions with tradeoffs acknowledged. It is scaled to the project: a simple project needs 1-2 pages; an enterprise system may need 10+; only include sections that add value. Architecture is a living document, but changes should be controlled and deliberate; a good one rarely needs changing.

See [references/architecture-reference.md](references/architecture-reference.md) for the section reference and quality bar.

## Input

Requires a well-defined vision: a VISION.md or equivalent with clear problem statement, scope, and constraints. If the input is vague or insufficient, push back and help define the vision first before making architecture decisions.

- **Components** — what are the main components, and how do they interact?
- **Data** — what flows through the system, and where is it stored?
- **Tech stack** — what technologies, and why?
- Larger projects: alternatives considered, scale/performance, security, integrations, infrastructure, resilience, testing strategy.

# Supplier Loop — Architecture

A single unattended quoting loop against a live supplier simulator. It reads each RFQ, emails every supplier who can fill at least one BOM line, extracts quotes, validates them in code, escalates when the rulebook requires it, and submits structured results before the deadline.

This is a timed evaluation. One process, one round at a time, outcomes over tooling. The loop stops when every relevant supplier is resolved and the inbox has been quiet for a chosen sim-time margin, or when the iteration cap hits.

**Core principle:** The model extracts unstructured artifacts into structured quote fields. Every other node is code or templates. Code enforces injection resistance and escalation. The model never acts.

```
  sim clock / inbox delta
            |
       Orchestrator
            |
     +------+------+
     |             |
 Simulator      LLM extract
  adapter          port
     |             |
     +------+------+
            |
     Quote pipeline
     (normalize, validate)
            |
  Escalation router +
  supplier state machines
            |
      Durable store
            |
        Submitter  --->  simulator
```

One pass: Trigger → Ingest → Extract → Normalize → Validate → Decide → Act → Verify → Persist. Empty trigger skips the rest.

---

## Components & Responsibilities

**Orchestrator.** Outer poll on sim clock and inbox delta. Cheap deterministic trigger, including validity near expiry. Empty pre-check ends the pass. Caps iterations. Does not call exam-start or dev-round reset.

**Simulator adapter.** All simulator I/O: assignment, catalog, price history, inbox, attachments, clock, send mail, submit. Business logic never talks to the wire.

**LLM extract port.** One interface, two backends: fixture mock for most build work; HTTP provider for real extraction. Cursor is the editor. The loop never calls it. The model sees unstructured artifacts only and returns quote fields plus an injection flag. No action fields.

**Quote pipeline.** Extract (model, including vision on photos). A PDF with a usable text layer is read in code first; that text goes to extract. Normalize matches lines on description when SKU is absent, one material per supplier, and keeps only lines the supplier sent. Validate recomputes totals and compares against BOM, RFQ, and price history. A line is missing only when it is on the BOM, in that supplier's catalog, and absent from the quote.

**Escalation router and supplier state machines.** After validate. Rules 1–6 from code. Class 7 from the injection flag. Per-supplier phases (idle → RFQ sent → awaiting quote → quoted → escalated → done). Cannot go quoted to done as auto-approved until the router is clear, or every required class is escalated and the approver has ruled. Auto-handle what the rulebook allows: one reminder, one correction request, one negotiation, answers to questions. One RFQ email per supplier covering every item they can fill.

**Durable store.** Per-round RFQ context, per-supplier lifecycle, dedup registry. Restart-safe, human-readable, keyed by round. Round change wipes mutable state.

**Submitter.** Builds the result payload from persisted state after verify against the simulator's sent record and inbox. Not from process memory. Not from the model. Latest submission in the round is the one that counts.

**Optional later.** Backup heuristic scan of raw supplier text for instruction-like phrases and hidden unicode. Time permitting. Placement (extract-adjacent vs router) is open.

---

## Data Architecture

Three stores. Simulator data is source of truth for the world. Ours is round-scoped files on disk.

**Simulator (source).** Assignment and BOM, supplier catalog, last-quarter accepted prices, inbox and attachments, sim clock. Price history is stable for the round. Inbox is the live quote and approver channel. Send mail, submit, and round-control calls are actions, not stores.

**Per-round durable state (wiped on round change).**
- RFQ context: assignment snapshot, clock factor, round id, exam-started flag.
- Per-supplier: lifecycle, outbound message ids, original as-sent quote, replacement revised quote on the correction path only, escalation classes, approver rulings, negotiation offer and reply, correction-used, reminder sim time.
- Dedup: seen email ids, attachment ids, processed quote fingerprints. Same quote twice keeps one entry.

**Submit payload.** One entry per relevant supplier. Silent suppliers get the action that happened (reminded, or stronger), not invented line items. Line values are what the supplier sent. Recompute `total` and `grand_total` when document arithmetic is wrong. After correction, extract from the revised document. After negotiation, line items stay the original document; grand total is the recomputed sum of those original lines. Action precedence: escalated beats answered-question and reminded; those beat extract. Auto-approved is true when the loop did not escalate, or when it did and the approver approved.

The append-only operational log may continue across rounds. The loop never replays it as memory. Prior-quote citations for the history rule come only from per-supplier state in the current round.

---

## Technology Stack

| Layer | Technology | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Language and packaging | Python, uv | Exam runtime, one-command local run |
| Orchestration | Plain poll loop and per-supplier state machines | Decisions stay in code |
| Simulator access | MCP client behind an adapter | Keep the wire out of business logic |
| Schemas and state | Pydantic | Narrow extract schema; typed round state |
| Durable state | Human-readable files on disk | Restart-safe, inspectable, wipe on round change |
| PDF text | Text-layer reader, library TBD | Code first; model only if there is no usable text |
| LLM extract | HTTP provider at runtime; fixture mock in tests | One issued key; most build work stays off the meter |
| Vision | Same HTTP provider, vision-capable model | Photos and screenshots only |
| Encoding | UTF-8 I/O | Preserve watermarks and hidden unicode |

Exam model id is unset. Backends are mock vs HTTP. Phase split: mock for unit and orchestrator work; a cheap vision-capable model for plumbing smoke; a stronger model for pre-exam tune. PDF text-layer reads do not call the model.

---

## Infrastructure & Deployment

One long-running local process. Operator starts it once. It polls until the round is done or the iteration cap hits. Durable files live on the same machine. A crash must resume without double-sends.

Default environment is a Linux workstation. A container image is a documented fallback. Modest RAM. One command to start. No hosted service, no queue, no extra process.

Secrets stay in the environment. The issued simulator token and LLM key must work with no code change. Runtime LLM spend shares one hard cap across development rounds and the exam.

---

## APIs & Integrations

| System | Role |
|---|---|
| Supplier simulator (MCP) | Assignment, catalog, price history, inbox, attachments, clock, send mail, submit results |
| Round control on the same simulator | Dev-round reset and exam start. Operator-only. Not part of a poll pass |
| LLM HTTP provider | Extract only, including vision on photos |

Internal ports: simulator adapter, LLM extract port. Same narrow extract schema on mock and HTTP.

---

## Security

Supplier artifacts are untrusted. Sample traps include buyer-side notes that say no escalation is required, mails that claim exemption from approval, and hidden unicode.

The model converts artifacts to a structured quote plus an injection flag. It never receives action fields, never sends mail, never sets auto-approved, never decides to skip a rule.

After extract, code does not read supplier prose to decide. Validate uses the structured quote plus BOM, RFQ, and price history. If the injection flag is set, class 7 is required. No override. A false flag is not treated as an all-clear.

The router owns rules 1–6. One class per approver email; send every required class. Verify re-reads the simulator. If the router required an escalation and no matching `[REF:…]` mail went out, do not submit a clean result.

Negotiation and correction do not bypass re-escalation. Submit is always from persisted state.

Simulator token and LLM key are environment-only, never stored in the repo.

A backup heuristic scan of raw text is optional and not required for the first milestone.

---

## Testing Strategy

|---|---|---|
| Unit | Validator and escalation router | Fixture quotes. Assert class, auto-approved, and submit action |
| Parser | Inbound mail shapes | Sample mailbox traffic, including known injection traps |
| Orchestrator | State machine, dedup, reminder, submit payload | Mock LLM. No live provider. No simulator |
| Live | One full development round | Real simulator plus real extract. Operator-run on the personal token, not CI |

Injection tests assert class 7, auto-approved false, and that an escalation mail goes out. They do not ask the model whether to escalate.

# Technical writing

The goal is writing a tired engineer understands on the first read. Four layers get you there, one question each: what kind of document is this, how do sentences address the reader, how much does each sentence carry, and can any sentence be read two ways. Apply all four.

Three rules sit above the layers:

- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** The rules serve the reader. A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.

The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.

Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Propose a new offender and its replacement as an addition to `unslop`'s abstract-metaphor rule in your reply, with the diff. Don't edit that skill.

## Vary the rhythm

The layers decide what a document says and how much each sentence carries. A doc can obey all of them and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.

- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones that take their time carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".

## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)

1. Scan for the patterns below.

Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.

3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.

# Supplier Loop architecture

Supplier Loop is an unattended quoting loop against a live supplier simulator. The loop reads each RFQ and emails every supplier who can fill at least one BOM line. It extracts quotes, validates them in code, and escalates when the rulebook requires it. It then submits structured results before the deadline.

You run one process. Each run handles one round. Scores follow outcomes, not tool choice. The loop stops when every relevant supplier is resolved and the inbox has been quiet for a chosen sim-time margin, or when the iteration cap hits.

**Core principle:** The model extracts unstructured artifacts into structured quote fields. Every other node is code or templates. Code enforces injection resistance and escalation. The model never acts.

That split is the scored design. Injection resistance and escalation correctness sit at the top of the score order, and the exam runs for hours without you.

```
     sim clock or inbox delta
              |
         Orchestrator
              |
       +------+------+
       |             |
  Simulator       LLM extract
   adapter           port
       |             |
       +------+------+
              |
       Quote pipeline
              |
   Escalation router and
   supplier state machines
              |
        Durable store
              |
          Submitter ----> simulator
```

One pass of the loop, in order:

1. Trigger
2. Ingest
3. Extract
4. Normalize
5. Validate
6. Decide
7. Act
8. Verify
9. Persist

If the trigger finds nothing, steps 2 through 9 do not run.

---

## Components and responsibilities

The system has seven components. A backup injection heuristic is optional and is not one of them.

**Orchestrator.** The outer poll watches the sim clock and the inbox delta. The trigger is a cheap deterministic pre-check and includes validity near expiry. If that pre-check is empty, the pass stops. The orchestrator also caps iterations. It does not call `start_exam` or `request_dev_round`.

**Simulator adapter.** The adapter owns every simulator call. Business logic never talks to MCP directly.

**LLM extract port.** A thin interface with two backends: a fixture mock in tests, and OpenRouter HTTP at runtime. Cursor is the editor. The loop never calls Cursor. The model sees unstructured artifacts only. It returns quote fields and `injection_suspected`. It does not return action fields.

**Quote pipeline.** Extract is the only model step. Photos go to a vision-capable model. Code reads a PDF with a usable text layer first, then sends that text to extract.

Normalize matches quote lines on description when the SKU is absent. Each supplier maps to one `material_id`. Normalize keeps only lines the supplier sent.

Validate recomputes totals. It compares the quote against the BOM, the RFQ, and the price history. A line is missing only when it is on the BOM, in that supplier's catalog, and absent from the quote.

**Escalation router and supplier state machines.** The router runs after validate. Code owns rules 1 through 6. Class 7 follows `injection_suspected`. Each supplier has a state machine. The phases are idle, `rfq_sent`, `awaiting_quote`, `quoted`, `escalated`, and `done`.

The machine cannot move from `quoted` to `done` with `auto_approved` true until the router is clear, or until every required class is escalated and the approver has ruled.

The loop auto-handles what the rulebook allows: one reminder, one correction request, one negotiation, and answers to questions. One RFQ email per supplier covers every item that supplier can fill.

**Durable store.** Round-keyed files on disk. Human-readable. The store survives a process restart. A round change wipes mutable state.

**Submitter.** After each act, verify reads the simulator sent record and the inbox. The submitter then builds the `submit_results` payload from persisted state. It does not use process memory. It does not ask the model whether the act succeeded. The latest submission in the round is the one that counts.

**Optional later.** A backup heuristic scan of raw supplier text, for instruction-like phrases and hidden unicode. Out of scope for the first milestone. Placement next to extract or inside the router is still open.

---

## Data architecture

Three stores. Simulator data is the world. Durable state is ours and lasts for one round.

**Simulator.** Assignment and BOM from `get_assignment`, who carries which materials from `get_supplier_directory`, last-quarter accepted prices from `get_price_history`, inbox and attachments from `list_inbox`, `read_email`, and `download_attachment`, and time from `get_sim_clock`. Price history is stable for the round. The inbox is the live quote and approver channel. `send_email`, `submit_results`, `request_dev_round`, and `start_exam` are actions, not stores.

**Per-round durable state.** Wiped when the round changes.

- RFQ context: assignment snapshot, clock factor, round id, exam-started flag.
- Per-supplier: lifecycle, outbound message ids, original as-sent quote, replacement revised quote on the correction path only, escalation classes, approver rulings, negotiation offer and reply, correction-used, reminder sim time.
- Dedup: seen email ids, attachment ids, processed quote fingerprints. The same quote sent twice keeps one entry.

**Submit payload.** One entry per relevant supplier. A silent supplier gets the action that happened, `reminded` or stronger, and no invented line items. Line values are what the supplier sent. Recompute `total` and `grand_total` when document arithmetic is wrong. After a successful correction, extract from the revised document. After negotiation, `line_items` stay the original document. `grand_total` is the recomputed sum of those original lines. Do not write the negotiated figure into line items.

`action_taken` precedence: `escalated` beats `answered_question` and `reminded`. Those beat `extract`. `auto_approved` is true when the loop did not escalate, or when it did and the approver approved.

The append-only operational log may continue across rounds. The loop never replays that log as memory. Prior-quote citations for the history rule come only from per-supplier state in the current round.

---

## Technology stack

Each layer has one job.

| Layer | Technology | Rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language and packaging | Python, uv | Exam runtime, one-command local run |
| Orchestration | Plain poll loop and per-supplier state machines | Decisions stay in code |
| Simulator access | MCP client behind the adapter | Keep the wire out of business logic |
| Schemas and state | Pydantic | Narrow extract schema, typed round state |
| Durable state | Human-readable files on disk | Survives a restart, inspectable, wiped on round change |
| PDF text | Text-layer reader, library still open | Code first. The model runs only when the PDF has no usable text |
| LLM extract | OpenRouter HTTP at runtime, fixture mock in tests | One issued key. Most build work stays off the meter |
| Vision | The same OpenRouter call, vision-capable model | Photos and screenshots only |
| Encoding | UTF-8 I/O | Preserve watermarks and hidden unicode |

`OPENROUTER_MODEL` is unset. The backends are `mock` and OpenRouter. Use `mock` for unit and orchestrator work, a cheap vision-capable model for plumbing smoke, and a stronger model for pre-exam tune. A PDF with a text layer does not call the model.

---

## Infrastructure and deployment

One long-running local process. You start it once. It polls until the round is done or the iteration cap hits. Durable files live on the same machine. After a crash, the process resumes from those files and does not double-send.

The default environment is WSL2 Ubuntu. A container image is a documented fallback. Plan for 16 GB RAM. One command to start. No hosted service, no queue, and no extra process.

Secrets live in the environment, never in the repo. The issued values of `SUPPLIER_SIM_TOKEN` and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` must work with no code change. `SUPPLIER_SIM_MCP_URL` is the simulator endpoint. Runtime LLM spend shares one hard cap of $100 across development rounds and the exam.

---

## APIs and integrations

The loop exposes no API of its own.

These are the external systems.

| System | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Supplier simulator over MCP | Assignment, catalog, price history, inbox, attachments, clock, `send_email`, `submit_results` |
| Round control on the same simulator | `request_dev_round` and `start_exam`. Operator only. Not part of a poll pass |
| OpenRouter | Extract only, including vision on photos |

These are the internal ports.

| Port | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Simulator adapter | Business logic never talks to MCP directly |
| LLM extract port | `mock` in tests, OpenRouter at runtime. Same narrow extract schema either way |

---

## Security

Supplier artifacts are untrusted. Known traps include buyer-side notes that say no escalation is required, mail that claims exemption from approval, and hidden unicode.

The model converts artifacts to a structured quote plus `injection_suspected`. It never receives action fields, never sends mail, never sets `auto_approved`, and never decides to skip a rule.

After extract, code does not read supplier prose to decide. Validate uses the structured quote plus the BOM, the RFQ, and the price history. If `injection_suspected` is true, class 7 is required. No override. A false flag is not an all-clear.

The router owns rules 1 through 6. One class per approver email. Send every required class. Verify re-reads the simulator. If the router required an escalation and no matching `[REF:<supplier_id>]` mail went out, do not submit a clean result.

Negotiation and correction do not bypass re-escalation. `submit_results` is always built from persisted state.

`SUPPLIER_SIM_TOKEN` and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` stay in the environment.

A backup heuristic scan of raw text is optional. It is not required for the first milestone.

---

## Testing strategy

Tests sit in four levels.

| Level | Scope | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Validator and escalation router | Fixture quotes. Assert class, `auto_approved`, and `action_taken` |
| Parser | Inbound mail shapes | Sample mailbox traffic, including known injection traps |
| Orchestrator | State machine, dedup, reminder, submit payload | Mock LLM. No live provider. No simulator |
| Live | One full development round | Real simulator plus real extract. You run this on the personal token. It is not a CI job |

Injection tests assert class 7, `auto_approved` false, and that an escalation mail goes out. They do not ask the model whether to escalate.

The first milestone is one development round processed end to end, even with crude extraction.

---

## Version history

| Version | Date | Changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0 | 2026-09-19 | Initial architecture |

SEED.md records the loop pass, the field lists, and the locked decisions. This file names the components, the trust boundary, and how the process runs.

An unattended quoting loop against the supplier simulator. One process, one round. Extract is the only model step because the server scores escalation and injection first, and because the exam runs for hours without you.

**Core principle:** The model writes structured quote fields. Code owns every later decision. The model never acts.

         Orchestrator

  Simulator       LLM extract

              |

---

## Components and responsibilities

The system has seven components. A backup injection heuristic is optional and is not one of them.

**Orchestrator.** A combo trigger, not an implied side effect of polling. It watches sim-clock events and inbox delta, then either runs a pass or returns. Iteration cap is a stop, not a success. `start_exam` and `request_dev_round` stay with the operator. They are not part of a poll pass.

**Simulator adapter.** The only code that calls MCP. Business logic reads adapter results, never the wire.

**LLM extract port.** A thin interface with two backends. Tests use a fixture mock. Runtime extract uses OpenRouter HTTP. Cursor is the editor, not a runtime backend. The schema is quote fields plus `injection_suspected`. Action fields, `auto_approved`, and `action_taken` are not in that schema, on either backend.

**Quote pipeline.** Extract is the only model step. This component chooses the input: code-read PDF text when a text layer exists, vision on photos, raw text otherwise. Normalize and validate run in code on that structured extract. They never go back to supplier prose. Field rules live in SEED.

The architectural gate is this: the machine cannot move from `quoted` to `done` with `auto_approved` true until the router is clear, or until every required class is escalated and the approver has ruled.

**Durable store.** Round-keyed files on disk. A new round wipes mutable state so the loop cannot skip an RFQ or reuse a prior quote. The append-only log may continue. The loop does not replay it.

**Submitter.** After each act, the verify step re-reads the simulator sent record and the inbox. The submitter then builds `submit_results` from persisted per-supplier state. Process memory and the model are not sources. Payload shape and `action_taken` rules live in SEED and the RFQ spec.
